To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the spatial decoherence of an optical beam in a random medium is initially linear with spatial separation, and then saturates, and (2) the spatial coherence is not a Gaussian random process, but is instead a nonstationary, nonergodic, non-Gaussian random process.
(1) We have measured the spatial decoherence (or correlation) of a wave field as it propagates in a random medium.
the transverse spatial coherence function of light in a random, multiple-scattering medium decays initially with a rate that increases with spatial separation and then saturates at large separation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the propagation of waves through random media and the associated problem of wave-field decoherence.
the propagation of light through a random medium.
the transport properties of wave fields in random multiple-scattering media.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the observed spatial decoherence is a consequence of the wave nature of light and that the saturation of the decoherence at large separations is a consequence of wave-field coherence and interference.
, for the first time, the saturation effect has been observed in a random multiple-scattering medium, and it can be modeled by a Boltzmann equation for the Winger function.
the Fokker–Planck model is not applicable for the case of a wave field propagating through a random medium, and the Boltzmann-like model is applicable for the same case.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the standard quantum mechanical theory of decoherence is not applicable for the description of the spatial decoherence of classical light waves in random media.

it is the first to provide experimental verification of the theoretical prediction that there is a saturation of the decoherence rate for a wave-field transport in a dense multiple scattering random medium.

the saturation of the decoherence rate in multiple-scattering media can be understood by considering the spatial coherence as an effective degree of freedom of the wave field and modeling the decoherence by a Boltzmann-type transport equation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatial decoherence in wave field transport in random multiple scattering media is a saturable phenomenon.
the saturation of the decoherence rate is a general feature of wave propagation in random media.
the spatial coherence of light can be measured in a dense, multiple scattering medium, and that this measurement provides information about the scattering medium itself.
